lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What's this, Alexander? Dead? Just like the rest of us?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: As you can see, Diogenes. Though it’s hardly surprising. I was human, so I died.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So Ammon was lying when he said you were his son? You were Philip's all along?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Obviously Philip's. If I were Ammon's son, I wouldn't be dead.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And what about all those stories they told about Olympias? A giant snake in her bed, her getting pregnant by a reptile... and Philip was just a dupe who thought you were his?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I heard the same stories you did. [sighs] Now I see that my mother and the prophets of Ammon were talking utter nonsense.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, it was a very useful lie for your career, Alexander. A lot of people cowered because they thought you were a god. [pause] But tell me—who did you leave that massive empire to?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I don't know, Diogenes. I never got around to making a will. All I managed to do was hand my signet ring to Perdiccas on my deathbed. [pause] Why are you laughing?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: [laughs] What do you think? I was just remembering the Greeks. The moment you took the throne, they were fawning over you, making you supreme commander against the barbarians. Some of them even added you to the twelve Olympian gods, building temples and sacrificing to the son of a snake! Anyway, tell me: where did the Macedonians bury you?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I'm actually still lying in Babylon. It's been thirty days. But Ptolemy, my bodyguard, promised that if he ever gets a break from the current chaos, he'll take me to Egypt and bury me there. So I can become one of the Egyptian gods.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: How can I not laugh, Alexander? Here you are in the underworld, still raving, still hoping you'll turn into Anubis or Osiris! Forget it, 'Your Divinity'. Nobody who crosses that lake and steps through those gates ever goes back. Aeacus runs a tight ship, and Cerberus isn't exactly a lapdog.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But here's what I'd really love to know. How do you handle it? Thinking about all that 'happiness' you left up there: the bodyguards, the shield-bearers, the satraps... the piles of gold, entire nations groveling at your feet. Babylon. Bactria. The war elephants! The glory of riding out in your purple cloak with a white ribbon tied around your head. Doesn't the memory just kill you? [pause] Are you crying? You idiot, didn't your wise tutor Aristotle ever teach you that the gifts of Fortune don't last?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: [crying] Wise? He was the worst sycophant of them all! Don't get me started on Aristotle. The things he begged me for, the letters he wrote... He completely played on my desire to be cultured. Flattering me, telling me my good looks were a 'philosophical good', praising my achievements, and my wealth! Oh, he definitely classified wealth as a 'good'—mostly so he wouldn't feel guilty about taking so much of mine. The man was a con artist, Diogenes. A total operator. And this is all I got from his 'wisdom': the sheer misery of realizing I've lost the 'greatest goods in life'. Which you just kindly listed for me.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell you what. I’ll prescribe you a cure for your grief. Since we don't grow hellebore down here, just march over to the river Lethe and start chugging. Drink, and then drink again. That'll cure your misery over Aristotle's 'goods'. [pause] Besides, I see Cleitus over there, and Callisthenes, and a whole mob of others heading this way. And they look like they want to tear you limb from limb for what you did to them. So take my advice: walk the other way, and keep drinking.
